newsitem.title: CANADA: ATHLETICS-CANADA'S BEN JOHNSON SUES TO RACE AGAIN.
newsitem.headline: ATHLETICS-CANADA'S BEN JOHNSON SUES TO RACE AGAIN.

text.p: Disgraced Canadian sprinter Ben Johnson launched a court action on Tuesday to win the right to race again and prove that he is still the world's fastest man.
The suit, filed in an Ontario court, alleges that Johnson's 1993 ban from international competition violated his ability to make a living.
"I just want to clear my name and to move on with my life," Johnson, 35, told a press conference in Toronto.
Johnson, a former world record holder in the 100 meters, was at the centre of the sport's most infamous doping case in 1988.

He won the gold medal at the Seoul Olympics after running the 100 meters in 9.79 seconds. But he was stripped of the medal and suspended from competition for two years after testing positive for an illegal steroid.

In 1993, Johnson was banned for life after a test found too much testosterone in his system. Johnson has denied using an illegal substance and his lawyers argued the IAAF did not give their client a fair hearing.
"The application before the Ontario court is based ... on the grounds that a lifetime ban of an athlete is contrary to the common law doctrine of restraint of trade," said lawyer Axy Leighl.
The Ontario court is scheduled to hear Johnson's application on May 27, a few days before an IAAF meeting.
Johnson's lawyer, said he hoped the IAAF would overturn the lifetime ban if the Ontario court ruled that Johnson's right to make a living had been violated.
"They (IAAF) have made earlier policy statements that they are willing to follow the rule in local jurisdictions. We hope that they adopt it," said Leighl.
Leighl said the IAAF was informed of Johnson's court action through its representative in Ottawa.
Johnson's mother Gloria said the lifetime ban on her son has been tough on the family.
"What my son went through I would never like to see another human being suffer as he did. It was really tough," said Gloria Johnson.

Johnson's lawyers said it was "strictly coincidence" that the court action was launched two weeks before a race in Toronto between Olympic sprint champions Donovan Bailey and Michael Johnson. The June 1 event is being billed as the race to decide who is the world's fastest man.

"We feel very strong that he (Ben Johnson) is competitive. He will talk with his legs when he's out there lining up against Donovan Bailey and Michael Johnson one of these days," said Johnson's agent Morris Chrobotek.
Asked by reporters who is the fleetest human being today, Johnson replied: "I'll tell you that: 9.79."

"The only thing those guys have right now is the competitive edge. They are in more racing shape than me, but as far as speed and power are concerned and mental endurance. I have that and I've trained harder than any athletes in the world today," he said.
The banned sprinter still draws a crowd at track events in Canada. At a track meet in Hamilton recently, Johnson signed autographs and posed for photos.
"When I walk on the street people say good luck or they hope to see me back. It's been very good," Johnson said of the public reaction to his effort to be reinstated.
